\chapter{La Casa Por Dentro}
\label{ch:es-casa-dentro}
\hlchaptermodality{432}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the machines and fittings a building notice talks about, and read a notice about the water being cut off.}

Read the notice or advert this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la lavadora]{la lavadora — the thing that washes}

\label{lesson:ES-C432-lavadora}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{lavar}. Say \emph{el proveedor}. You met the doer-ending one chapter ago. Put it on \emph{lavar} and guess before you are told.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la lavadora}
\textbf{la lavadora} — the washing machine.

If you guessed it, that is the point of the last chapter arriving before this one.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lavar} plus \textbf{-dora}. The same ending as \textbf{el proveedor}, in its feminine form, and it does the same job — except that here the doer is a machine rather than a person.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the doer} \\
\midrule
lavar & la lavadora \\
secar & la secadora \\
calcular & la calculadora \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Spanish names most household machines this way, so \textbf{-dora} is worth more to you than any single appliance. A machine that does something is usually that something plus this ending, and you can often reach the word without having met it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la lavadora}
  \item the verb it was built from
  \item what a machine for drying would be called
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The washing machine? (\textbf{la lavadora}.) The ending? (\textbf{-dora}.) Where did you meet it first? (\textbf{On the supplier.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el contador]{el contador — the thing that counts}

\label{lesson:ES-C432-contador}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{contar}. Say \emph{la lavadora}. Do the same move again: the ending on the verb, and say what the machine must be.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el contador}
\textbf{el contador} — the meter. The box that counts your water, your gas, your electricity.

\textbf{contar} carries two senses you already hold — to count, and to tell a story. The meter takes the counting one.

\begin{cousinweb}
Twice in two lessons the same ending has handed you a word. That is worth pausing on, because it is the difference between a vocabulary you memorise and one you can extend.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you know} & \textbf{you can reach} \\
\midrule
lavar & la lavadora \\
contar & el contador \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{el contador del agua} is the phrase you will actually meet, on notices about somebody coming to read it. Note the gender: this one is masculine where the washing machine was feminine, and nothing about the ending decides that — the machine takes whatever gender its own word already had.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el contador}
  \item the water meter
  \item the two things \emph{contar} can mean
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The meter? (\textbf{el contador}.) Built from? (\textbf{contar}.) And the washing machine? (\textbf{la lavadora}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la estantería]{la estantería — a place full of shelves}

\label{lesson:ES-C432-estanteria}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el contador}. That ending has now served you twice. Here is a different one, and it does a different job.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la estantería}
\textbf{la estantería} — the shelving, the bookcase, the shelf unit.

A single shelf is \textbf{el estante}. The \textbf{-ería} makes it the whole structure.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{-ería} does not make a doer. It makes a \textbf{place or collection} of the thing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the thing} & \textbf{the place or collection} \\
\midrule
el estante & la estantería \\
el pan & la panadería \\
el libro & la librería \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is why so many shop names end this way: a \emph{panadería} is where the bread is, a \emph{librería} where the books are. Meeting the ending once tells you what a shop sells before you have read the sign properly.

Two endings, two different jobs: \textbf{-dor} gives you who or what does it, \textbf{-ería} gives you where it is kept.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la estantería}
  \item one shelf, then the whole unit
  \item where you would buy bread, using the ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The shelving? (\textbf{la estantería}.) One shelf? (\textbf{el estante}.) What does \textbf{-ería} add? (\textbf{The place or collection.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la tubería]{la tubería — all the pipes together}

\label{lesson:ES-C432-tuberia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la estantería}. Say \emph{el agua}. A \textbf{tubo} is a pipe. Say what a \emph{tubería} must be before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la tubería}
\textbf{la tubería} — the pipework, the plumbing, the run of pipes.

\textbf{el tubo} is one pipe. The ending collects them, exactly as it collected the shelves.

\begin{cousinweb}
Third time for an ending in two chapters, and the second time for this one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{one} & \textbf{the collection} \\
\midrule
el estante & la estantería \\
el tubo & la tubería \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the word in the notice that says the water is being cut off: \emph{reparar una tubería}. The repair is to the \textbf{run of pipes}, not to one length of tube, and the word chooses itself accordingly.

If you are keeping count, you have now reached four words in this chapter and three of them you could have guessed from a piece you already had.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la tubería}
  \item one pipe, then all of them
  \item they are repairing a pipe and cutting off the water
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The pipework? (\textbf{la tubería}.) One pipe? (\textbf{el tubo}.) Which other word this chapter used the same ending? (\textbf{la estantería}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el sofá]{el sofá — the one you could not guess}

\label{lesson:ES-C432-sofa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la silla}. You can name one seat. Name the long soft one that three people share.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el sofá}
\textbf{el sofá} — the sofa.

Stressed on the last syllable, \emph{so-FÁ}, and the written accent is there to say so.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{This one was not built from anything you hold.} Four words in this chapter came apart into a piece plus an ending; this one did not, and pretending otherwise would waste your time.

It came into Spanish from Arabic, where the word named a raised, cushioned bench along a wall. Spanish took hundreds of words from Arabic over several centuries, and they tend to arrive \textbf{whole} like this rather than as pieces you can recombine.

So the honest lesson of the chapter is two-sided:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when a word comes apart} & \textbf{when it does not} \\
\midrule
look for the ending first & learn it whole, and move on \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Knowing which kind you are looking at is the skill. Trying to decompose \emph{sofá} would cost you minutes and teach you nothing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el sofá}
  \item a chair, then a sofa
  \item which syllable takes the stress
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The sofa? (\textbf{el sofá}.) Could you have built it from a piece you had? (\textbf{No.}) Where did it come from? (\textbf{Arabic.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(lavadora, contador, estantería …]{(lavadora, contador, estantería, tubería, sofá) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R432-repaso-casa}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{the washing machine}, \emph{the meter} and \emph{the sofa}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two endings and one exception}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{built from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la lavadora} & lavar + \textbf{-dora} \\
\textbf{el contador} & contar + \textbf{-dor} \\
\textbf{la estantería} & estante + \textbf{-ería} \\
\textbf{la tubería} & tubo + \textbf{-ería} \\
\textbf{el sofá} & nothing — borrowed whole \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four of five came apart. Do not read a rule into it — the next five household words might all be whole. What this chapter is for is the \textbf{question}, asked before you reach for a dictionary: \emph{is there a piece in here I already have?}

The two endings answer different questions. \textbf{-dor} and \textbf{-dora} name the one that does it. \textbf{-ería} names where the thing is kept or collected.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could name a house and a chair, and almost nothing inside either.} \emph{La casa}, \emph{la silla} and \emph{el agua} have been yours for a long time. What was missing was everything a notice on a door actually talks about: the meter somebody comes to read, the pipework they are repairing, the machine that broke.

You now hold the vocabulary of the \textbf{building}, not only of the home.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five words
  \item which one you could not have built
  \item the two endings and what each one does
  \item they are repairing the pipework and reading the water meter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The shelving? (\textbf{la estantería}.) The pipework? (\textbf{la tubería}.) And the one that came in whole? (\textbf{el sofá}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(un aviso a los vecinos) — the notice on the door}

\label{lesson:ES-C432-sintesis-aviso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la tubería} and \emph{el agua}. You are about to read the notice those two words exist for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read it once straight through, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{AVISO A LOS VECINOS} El martes cortaremos el \textbf{agua} entre las nueve y las dos para reparar una \textbf{tubería} del garaje. El miércoles vendrán a leer los \textbf{contadores}.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what happens on Tuesday and for how long
  \item what is being repaired
  \item what happens the following day
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now say these aloud, as if telling somebody who has not read the notice:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item on Tuesday there is no water in the morning
  \item they are repairing a pipe in the garage
  \item I cannot put the washing machine on until the afternoon
  \item so I am reading on the sofa until they finish
\end{itemize}

\textbf{A notice like this one is where a beginner's Spanish usually stops.} Every word in it is ordinary and none of it is in a textbook dialogue. You can read it now, and you could not two chapters ago.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are they repairing? (\textbf{una tubería}.) What are they coming to read? (\textbf{los contadores}.) What can you not use that morning? (\textbf{la lavadora}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
